The Confederates then tried to send their soldiers into eastern Kentucky in the fall of 1862 but lost the Battle of Perryville and then left Kentucky. Over the next year, the Union took control of the rest of Tennessee. The North won control of almost all of the Mississippi River by capturing the cities along the river in the fall of 1862 and the spring of 1863. However, the Confederacy still held Vicksburg, an important city and fort. If they held, the Confederates could move soldiers and supplies from one side of the river to the other. Grant started the Siege of Vicksburg during the month of May 1863. The siege continued until July 4, 1863, when the Confederates there surrendered to Grant. That was one of the turning points in the war by dividing the Confederacy into two parts. There were also battles west of the Mississippi River Valley in the Trans-Mississippi Theater. For example, two important battles were the Battle of Wilson's Creek and the Battle of Pea Ridge. The Confederates tried to invade New Mexico in February and March 1862 but they were defeated at the Battle of Glorieta Pass. After the Union captured Vicksburg, the area became separated from the rest of the Confederate States. Other battles happened in the area after the capture of Vicksburg. During the Siege of Vicksburg in the west, another turning point came in the east. After winning some battles, Lee decided to invade the North again. Lee and his Army of Northern Virginia went into Pennsylvania. The Confederate Army met the Union Army near Gettysburg, Pennsylvania and fought the Battle of Gettysburg, which lasted from July 1 to 3, 1863. More soldiers died at Gettysburg than in any other Civil War battle, which the Union won. Lee and his troops were pushed back into the South and could no longer invade the North. From Vicksburg, Grant led the army to finish taking control of Tennessee in the Chattanooga campaign. Lincoln then decided that Grant was his best general and put Grant in control of all Union armies. Abraham Lincoln also made William Tecumseh Sherman the general in charge leading the Union troops from Tennessee to Georgia. Grant led many attacks on Lee's army in Virginia. The battles were made up the Overland Campaign. The Union had more success when Sherman marched into Georgia in May 1864, into the middle of the Confederate States. In September, he captured Atlanta, an important city. Sherman then led a "march to the sea" and captured Savannah. He then marched north through South Carolina and North Carolina. Confederate General Joseph E. Johnston attacked Sherman at the Battle of Bentonville. Sherman won the battle. Even in the 20th century, Southerners remember Sherman's march as destroying many homes, farms, and railroads, but his soldiers are blamed for things that they could not have done since they were too far away. By late 1864, Lee's army was struggling, as they had less soldiers and supplies than Grant's army. Helped by Philip Sheridan, Grant's army slowly started to push into Virginia. At the start of April 1865, they won several battles against Lee's army and captured Richmond. Lee decided that he had too few soldiers to keep on fighting. He surrendered to Grant on April 9, 1865 near Appomattox Court House. Later, many other Confederate armies surrendered as well. The last Confederate general to surrender was Brigadier General Stand Watie, who surrendered on June 23, 1865, in Oklahoma. After the war ended, Lincoln pardoned all of the Confederate soldiers and so they could not be arrested or punished for fighting against the Union. The South would be allowed to rejoin the United States but only later. Some Confederates did not want to return to the United States and moved to places like Mexico or Brazil. Historians have had different ideas about whether the Confederacy could have won the war. Most of them, such as James McPherson, say that it would have been difficult but possible. The Union had far more people, money and industry. By most estimates, the Union had over 2 million soldiers while the Confederacy had 1 million. One advantage the Confederacy had was that they only needed to defend their land, whereas the Union could only win if they took full control of the Confederate states. Furthermore, the Union could only fight the war if their people wanted them to keep fighting. Lincoln had opponents in the North (the Copperheads) who wanted the war to end. If the Confederacy had defended itself for long enough, it may have led to more people in the Union turning against the war and supporting the Copperheads. However, Lincoln held on to his support and won the 1864 election. The Union Navy blocked ships from going into the Confederate ports. Although some ships managed to get past, most could not. The Confederacy had big money problems because they could not sell cotton and other goods to other countries. The Confederacy collected less taxes than the Union, so they printed money to pay for the war. This caused inflation (rising prices). Another factor was that the Confederacy could not get help from outside. They had hoped that Britain and France would support the Confederacy because they wanted to buy their cotton. However, Britain and France did not give them help. There were three reasons for this. Firstly, they thought that slavery was wrong. Secondly, they did not want to become enemies of the United States. Thirdly, they could get cotton from elsewhere. Most historians also think that Abraham Lincoln was a better leader than Jefferson Davis. Don E. Fehrenbacher says that Lincoln's skills helped keep the Border States and ordinary people on his side. Lincoln left his generals alone if they did a good job and fired them if they did not. Davis lacked a clear plan, tried to do too many tasks at once and often chose people to do jobs just because they were his friends. He annoyed his generals and other Confederate politicians. William Cooper says that better leadership helped the Union, but they were already more likely to win. Many soldiers on both sides died during the war. Most of the war was fought in the South. Many railroads, farms, houses and other things were destroyed, and most people living there became very poor. After the war, some of the Union Army's leaders went into politics. Generals like Grant, Hayes, Garfield, Harrison, and McKinley became US presidents. Other veterans were elected to other offices. The period after the war, called Reconstruction, lasted from the end of the war to 1877. The Union Army stayed in some Southern states and made them occupied territory. During Reconstruction, black Americans built schools and other social infrastructure. Some of the schools became the historically black colleges that still exist. After southern states rejoined the Union, most of them made laws that limited what black people could do. The Southern states were allowed to ask to rejoin the union. After they were accepted, they could send senators and representatives to the US Congress again and make their own state laws. The Amnesty Act of 1872 restored the rights to vote and to hold political office for most former members of the Confederacy. Some of them also became politicians. Three important amendments were added on to the US Constitution. The amendments were suggested by the US government. Although not every American supported them, they got enough support to pass. The Thirteenth Amendment says that slavery is not allowed anywhere in the United States. This completed the work of the Emancipation Proclamation. The Fourteenth Amendment makes it clear that all people born in the United States are citizens, and all citizens have equal rights. The Fifteenth Amendment says that people in the United States cannot be kept from voting because of their race.

The American Cancer Society (founded in 1913) is a nonprofit organization, divided into six geographic areas with over 250 regional offices around the US. In 1913, ten doctors and five businessmen established the "American Society for the Control of Cancer" (ASCC) in New York City. The Better Business Bureau listed American Cancer Society as an accredited charity meeting all of its Standards for Charity Accountability. In 2020, the American Cancer Society introduced a charity internet stream series Gamers Vs. Cancer. In 2011, the American Cancer Society came under fire for denying Foundation Beyond belief, a nonreligious charity, entry into its Relay For Life "National Team" program.

The American Health Care Act of 2017 (H.R. 1628), referred to by the acronym AHCA and nicknamed variously as Trumpcare, Ryancare, Republicare, and pejoratively Obamacare-Lite, is a United States Congress bill to repeal and replace the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act "Obamacare" (ACA). It is based on a plan first publicly released by House Republicans on March 6, 2017, and the first part of what is a 3-phase plan to repeal the act. Consideration of the bill was postponed on March 24, 2017, after it failed to gain enough House Republican support to pass it. Towards the end of April 2017, Republicans began trying to revive the bill with the MacArthur Amendment, named after Representative Tom MacArthur of New Jersey. On May 4, 2017, the United States House of Representatives voted in favor of repealing the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act and passing the American Health Care Act with a narrow vote of 217 to 213, sending the bill to the Senate for a full majority vote.

American Pharoah (born 2011; foaled February 2, 2012) is an American Thoroughbred racehorse. He won the American Triple Crown and the Breeders' Cup Classic in 2015. In winning all four races, he became the first horse to win the "Grand Slam" of American horse racing. He won the 2015 Eclipse Award for Horse of the Year and 2015 Champion three-year-old. He was bred and owned throughout his racing career by Ahmed Zayat of Zayat Stables, trained by Bob Baffert, and ridden in most of his races by Victor Espinoza. He now stands at stud at Ashford Stud in Kentucky. His sire was Pioneerof the Nile and his dam was Littleprincessemma.
The American Music Award for New Artist of the Year has been awarded since 2004. Before, the award was known as Favorite Breakthrough Artist (2004) and Breakthrough Artist (2005–2010).

Amerigo Vespucci (9 March 1451- 22 February 1512) was an Italian merchant, explorer and cartographer. He was the first person to explain that the places discovered by Christopher Columbus in 1492 were not part of east Asia, but an unknown continent which he called "The New World". America got its name when other cartographers used a feminized and latinized version of his first name, Americus. Not much is known of Vespucci's life. Two books were published saying he wrote them. Some letters exist, also saying he wrote them. He visited the New World at least twice, and died of malaria.

Al-Ustaj Umbra Amiril Kato (18 May 1946 – 14 April 2015) was a Filipino terrorist. He was the founder of the Bangsamoro Islamic Freedom Fighters (BIFF) a group which seceded from Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF). He joined the MILF after 1985, after he graduated from Imam Muhammad bin Saud Islamic University in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. Umbra Kato was the Philippine's most wanted man though due to his still official membership in the MILF. Kato died of a heart attack at the age of 68.

Amfilohije Radović (;; 7 January 1938 – 30 October 2020) was a bishop of the Serbian Orthodox Church. He was first the Bishop of Banat between 1985 and 1990, and then the Metropolitan Bishop of Montenegro and the Littoral from 1990, until his death. He was born in Bare Radovića, Kingdom of Yugoslavia. On 7 October 2020, Radović was tested positive for COVID-19. He died on 30 October 2020 from the infection at a hospital in Podgorica, Montenegro at the age of 82.

Aminah Brenda Lynn Robinson (February 18, 1940 – May 22, 2015) was an American artist. Robinson received her formal art training at the Columbus Art School (now the Columbus College of Art and Design). She was known for creating sculptures in Columbus neighborhoods. Robinson died on May 22, 2015 from heart failure, aged 75.

Amina al-Said (January 20, 1914 - August 13, 1995) was an Egyptian feminist, journalist, and editor. In 1931, she was one of the first three women to graduate from Fu’ad University. She advocated for women's rights in Egypt. She started the first Arabic magazine for women in 1934, the Hawaa-Eve. She also helped start the Pan-Arab Feminist Union. Al-Said was the first Egyptian journalist to be paid by a major publisher. She received the First State Recognition Award, First Order of the Republic, Universal Star, and National Arts Award. She was also one of the first women's rights activists to be supported by her government.

Aminul Islam (born 29 December 1963) is a poet and essayist. He is from Bangladesh. Aminul has written seventeen books. He written thirteen poetry books. He has been involved in creative writing for 20 years. Bishwayan, Bangla Kabita O Onnyannyo Probandha (collection of essays)

Amir Ganiel (January 6, 1963 – May 14, 2018) was an Israeli swimming champion and record holder in swimming. He was part of the in the World Championships in Berlin for the national team. He worked in long distance. He was called one of the greatest Israeli swimmers. He became a surgeon, after his swimming career. Ganiel was born and died in Jerusalem.

Aminu Ado Bayero (born 21 August 1961) is the 15th Fulani Emir of Kano from the Fulani Sullubawa clan. Bayero holds bachelor's degree in mass communication from Bayero University Kano and master's degree from Flying College, Oakland, California, US. He did his one-year mandatory National Youth Service Corps at the Nigeria Television Authority in Makurdi.

Amish friendship bread is a type of bread or cake made from a sourdough starter that is often shared in a manner similar to a chain letter. The starter is a replacement for baking yeast. It can be used to make many kinds of yeast-based breads, shared with friends, or frozen for future use. The sweet, cake-like Amish cinnamon bread is a common bread that is made from this starter. It is a simple, stirred quickbread. It includes a large amount of sugar and vegetable oil, with a mild cinnamon flavor. It has characteristics of both pound cake and coffee cake. The flavor of the finished product can be changed by not using cinnamon. A common recipe using this starter uses one cup (240 ml) of it to make bread. A second cup is saved to start a new cycle. The remaining two cups are given to friends. The process of sharing the starter makes it somewhat like a chain letter. One cup of starter makes one standard loaf of bread. It can also be called German friendship cake, or "Herman" the German friendship cake. The starter mix can be made from a recipe of flour, water and yeast. One cup of the mixture is then passed to other people who get instructions on how to keep it alive, usually just saying to give it more ingredients as time passes.

Amita Marie Nicolette Berthier (born 15 December 2000) is a foil fencer from Singapore. She won four medals at the NCAA Fencing Championships. She also won three gold medals at the Southeast Asian Games. In April 2021, Berthier took part in the 2020 Summer Olympics after winning a tournament in Tashkent, Uzbekistan. In 2023, Berthier won a bronze medal at the 2023 Asian Fencing Championships in Wuxi, China. She was also a flag carrier in Hangzhou, China. In 2024, Berthier took part in the 2024 Olympics. She was 28th place. Later, she went to Washington, D.C. for a competition, where she was 20th place.

Amotz Zahavi (January 1, 1928 – May 12, 2017) was an Israeli evolutionary biologist, a Professor in the Department of Zoology at Tel Aviv University, and one of the founders of the Society for the Protection of Nature in Israel (known as the "SPNI"). His main work was about the evolution of signals, particularly those signals that are indicative of fitness, and their selection for "honesty". He was born in Petah Tikva, Israel. Zahavi died in Tel Aviv, Israel on May 12, 2017, aged 89.

Amos Adams Lawrence (July 31, 1814August 22, 1886), the son of philanthropist Amos Lawrence, was an important person in the United States abolition movement shortly before the Civil War. He was important in building the University of Kansas in Lawrence, Kansas and Lawrence University in Appleton, Wisconsin. Lawrence was born in Boston, Massachusetts on July 31, 1814. He died at his summer resort in Nahant, Massachusetts on August 22, 1886. Lawrence gave a lot of money to the New England Emigrant Aid Company because he did not want slavery. He gave guns to Jayhawkers to help them fight in the Civil War. Lawrence's parents were Unitarians, but he became Anglican and was confirmed as a member of St. Paul's Episcopal Church in Boston in 1842. He met and married Sarah Elizabeth Appleton (1822–1891) at the church. Sarah was a daughter of U.S. Representative William Appleton and Mary Ann Appleton (née Cutler). His mother was a relative of Samuel Appleton, a trustee of Massachusetts General Hospital and president of the Young Men's Benevolent Society. Amos and his wife, Sarah, had four children. They were: William Lawrence (1850–1941), who became the Bishop of Massachusetts. Harriet Lawrence Hemenway (1858-1960), who became a co-founder of the Massachusetts Audubon Society. He died at his summer resort in Nahant, Massachusetts.

Amrish Tyagi (born 14 February 1978) is an Indian political strategist. He is the son of K.C. Tyagi. He worked for Donald Trump, helped with giving the demands, and for the Asian community in the United States, transport this to Trump's team, and to design to achieve goal to messages to draw the community in, and create datas for Trump's goal.

Ali Amrozi bin Haji Nurhasyim (also known as Amrozi; 5 July 1962 - 9 November 2008) was an Indonesian who was convicted for his part in the 2002 Bali terrorist bombing. He was executed along with two other men involved in the bombing in early November 2008. Ali was executed on November 9 by a firing squad.

Amrita Sher-Gil (30 January 1913 – 5 December 1941) was a famous Indian artist and painter. She was born to a Punjabi Sikh father and a Hungarian mother. Because of her life and work, she is sometimes known as 'India's Frida Kahlo'.She was born into Majitha royal family. She is considered an important woman painter of 20th century India. She died in 1941 in Lahore city, now in Pakistan, at the age of 28.

Amritlal Vegad (3 October 1928 – 6 July 2018) was an Indian writer and poet. He wrote in Gujarati and Hindi from Jabalpur. Amritlal Vegad was awarded in 2004 with Sahitya Akademi Award for his travelogue – Saundaryani Nadi Narmada and also Madhya Pradesh Rajya Sahitya Award & Rashtrapati Award for his various works. He was best known for his novel Narmada-ki-pari-krama written in Hindi language and Saundaryani Nadi Narmada (travelogue) & Parikramā Narmadā maiyānī in Gujarati language. Vegad died on 6 July 2018 from respiratory failure at the age of 89.

Amrita Pritam (31 August 1919 – 31 October 2005) was an Indian novelist and poet, who wrote in Punjabi and Hindi. She is the recipient of the 1956 Sahitya Akademi Award. She wrote more than 100 books of poetry, fiction, biographies, essays, a collection of Punjabi folk songs and an autobiography that were all translated into several Indian and foreign languages. Pritam was born on August 31, 1919, in Gujranwala, Punjab, British India. She was the only child of Raj Bibi, who was a school teacher, and Kartar Singh Hitkari, who was a poet, a scholar of the Braj Bhasha language, and the editor of a literary journal. She was known for her powerful and emotional poetry that often portrayed the struggles of women and the partition of India. Her writing continues to inspire generations of readers with its themes of love, loss, and social injustice. She started her journey as a romantic poet and soon became part of the Progressive Writers' Movement. The effect was seen in her collection, Lok Peed ("People's Anguish", 1944), which openly criticised the war-torn economy after the Bengal famine of 1943. She was also involved in social work. She also worked at a radio station in Lahore for a while, before the partition of India. She passed away on October 31, 2005 after a long sickness but her legacy lives on through her timeless words.

Amy Smith is an American inventor, educator, and founder of D-Lab at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Her work focuses on development of appropriate technologies. Appropriate technologies are technologies that use readily available local resources to solve problems in developing countries. Amy Smith was born in Lexington, Massachusetts, on 4 November 1962.

Ambrose of Dorostol (born Alexander Alexandrov Parashkevov; 9 June 1942 – 18 August 2020) was a Bulgarian Orthodox clergyman. He was the Bishop of Branitsa from 1998 to 2010 and Metropolitan of Dorostol from 2010 to his death in 2020. He was a member of the Bulgarian Orthodox Church. Dorostolski died from COVID-19 on 18 August 2020 in Silistra at the age of 78.

Amy Elizabeth Fisher (born August 21, 1974) is an American woman. She became known in the media as the Long Island Lolita in 1992. That year, at age seventeen, she shot Mary Jo Buttafuoco, the wife of Joey Buttafuoco. She was originally charged with attempted murder. Fisher later pleaded guilty to first-degree aggravated assault. She was in prison for just under seven years. In 1999, she was paroled. Fisher later became a writer, webcam model and a pornographic actress. Fisher became very jealous of Joey Buttafuoco's wife. Fisher then got a.25 caliber handgun. When the wife answered the door, Fisher told her that Joey Buttafuoco was having an affair with Fisher's (imaginary) younger sister. The conversation lasted 15 minutes. Mary Jo got angry. She then told Fisher to leave and turned her back to return to the house. That was when Fisher took out the gun, struck Mary Jo with it and shot her in the head. Fisher dropped the gun and the shirt. She came back for them. The police interviewed Joey Buttafuoco. He told them Amy Fisher could be the shooter. When his wife, Mary Jo became conscious, she identified Fisher as the shooter. Amy Fisher was born in Merrick, New York. Fisher, Amy & Robbie Woliver (2004). If I Knew Then. iUniverse.. Fisher, Amy with Sheila Weller (1994). Amy Fisher: My Story. (Reprint edition.). (Originally published by Pocket Books in 1993;.) Dominguez, Pier (2001). Amy Fisher: Anatomy of a Scandal: The Myth, the Media and the Truth Behind the Long Island Lolita Story. Writers Club Press.. Eftimiades, Maria (1992). Lethal Lolita: A True Story of Sex, Scandal and Deadly Obsession. St. Martin's Press.. Amy Fisher: My Story, 1992 (TV) Noelle Parker starred as Fisher. Casualties of Love: The "Long Island Lolita" Story, 1993 (TV) Alyssa Milano starred as Fisher. The Amy Fisher Story, 1993 (TV) Drew Barrymore starred as Fisher. According to Alan Ball, Fisher's story was an inspiration to him in writing the script for the 1999 film American Beauty.

Amy Tan (born February 19, 1952) is an American writer. Her works deal with mother-daughter relationships. Her most well-known work is The Joy Luck Club. It has been translated into 35 languages. In 1993, a movie was made based on the book. Tan has written several other novels. These include The Kitchen God's Wife, The Hundred Secret Senses, The Bonesetter's Daughter and Saving Fish from Drowning. She also wrote a collection of non-fiction essays entitled The Opposite of Fate: A Book of Musings. Her novel Saving Fish from Drowning explores the problems dealt with by a group of people who disappear while on an art expedition in the jungles of Burma. Tan has also written two children's books: The Moon Lady (1992) and Sagwa, the Chinese Siamese Cat (1994). Sagwa was turned into an animated series which aired on PBS. She also appeared on PBS in a short spot encouraging children to write. She is a child of Chinese immigrants: John and Daisy Tan.

Amy Krouse Rosenthal (April 29, 1965 – March 13, 2017) was an American author of both adult and children's books, a short filmmaker, and former radio show host. Rosenthal was born in Chicago, Illinois. She graduated at Tufts University. She married Jason Brian Rosenthal. They had three children. She was best known for her memoir Encyclopedia of an Ordinary Life, her children's picture books, and the movie project The Beckoning of Lovely. She was a prolific writer, publishing over 30 children's books between 2005 and her death in 2017. She is the only author to have three children's books make the Best Children's Books for Family Literacy list in the same year. She was a contributor to Chicago's NPR affiliate WBEZ and to the TED conference. Rosenthal died in Chicago, Illinois from ovarian cancer on March 13, 2017, aged 51.
Amy Goodman (born April 13, 1957) is an American broadcast journalist, columnist, investigative reporter, and author. Since 1996, she has been the main host of Democracy Now!.

Amy Uyematsu (October 18, 1947 – June 23, 2023) was a Japanese American poet who has written six highly acclaimed poetry collections. Prominent writer Naomi Hirahara called Uyematsu, "One of LA's finest poets." Her writing mainly focused on the discrimination she experienced as both an Asian-American and a woman. Much of her early work explored the origins of the yellow power movement, which was a campaign inspired by the Black Power movement that worked towards equal rights for Asian Americans. Uyematsu won the Nicholas Roerich Poetry Prize for her first book, 30 Miles from J-Town, in 1992. She attended UCLA during the late 1960s and early 1970s, where she began writing poetry in response to anti-Asian racism in the U.S. that was largely caused by the ongoing Vietnam War. Uyematsu’s activism spurred her to help start up UCLA’s Asian American Studies Program immediately after her graduation. Her writing appeared in many anthologies and journals published internationally. Her essay from 1969, “The Emergence of Yellow Power in America,” has had a lasting impact on Asian-American studies across the country, through her criticism of social inequities: “Although the race situation in America is not strictly analogous to white colonialism and imperialism, the blacks and yellows have suffered similar consequences as Third World people at the hands of the American capitalist power.” Uyematsu was also an experienced educator and taught high school mathematics for over thirty years in Los Angeles.

Amy Euphemia Jacques Garvey (31 December 1895 – 25 July 1973) was a journalist, feminist, and race activist. In 1918, she started working in the Universal Negro Improvement Association and African Communities League (UNIA). and became Marcus Garvey’s personal secretary. She later became the office manager at U.N.I.A. headquarters in 1920. Two years later, in July 1922, Amy Jacques and Marcus Garvey married, following his divorce from Amy Ashwood. Jacques was dedicated to spreading information on the principles (principles - a basic law or truth on which action or behavior is based) and philosophies (philosophy - a way of thinking about the world, the universe, and society) of race and self-reliance (self-reliance - relying on your own abilities and resources instead of someone else's). On June 21, 1922, her husband was convicted of mail fraud and sent to prison. During this time, Jacques took leadership of the U.N.I.A. and acted as his personal representative. She rallied (rallied - to call people together for a common effort) to his defense, made speeches to U.N.I.A. branches, and met with U.N.I.A. officers and public officials. Marcus Garvey had asked Jacques to edit two volumes of his Philosophy and Opinions and to distribute them to members of the United States Congress, so in 1923, Jacques published Volume One of The Philosophy and Opinions of Marcus Garvey. Volume Two came out in 1925. She additionally became the associate editor of the U.N.I.A.’s newspaper and created a page called “Our Women and What They Think." This section had information on the status of women and profiles of black female leaders/historical figures. With these publications, she raised money for her husband’s legal defense. However, Marcus Garvey was deported (deported - to force someone who is not a citizen to leave the country) and had to go back to Jamaica. Jacques returned with him and their children, Marcus Garvey Jr. and Julius Garvey. She still continued to contribute to the U.N.I.A.’s newspaper, and wrote about her impressions of England, France, and Germany as she toured the countries with her husband. After her husband’s death in 1940, she continued to fight for African independence and became a contributing editor to the African, a black nationalist (nationalist - strongly identifying with their own nation) journal. She also started the African Study Circle of the World in Jamaica in the 1940s and published the book Garvey and Garveyism in 1963. Amy Jacques Garvey died on July 25, 1973 in Kingston, Jamaica, the same place where she was born.

Amélie Nothomb (born Fabienne-Claire on 9 July 1966) is a Belgian writer who writes in French. Amélie Nothomb was born in Etterbeek, Belgium to Belgian diplomats. She lived in Japan, then in China, New York, Bangladesh, Burma, Coventry and Laos. Nothomb's first novel, Hygiène de l'assassin, was published in 1992. Since then, she has published about one novel per year, including Les Catilinaires (1995), Fear and Trembling (1999) and Métaphysique des tubes (2000, published in English as The Character of Rain). She has been awarded many prizes, including the 1999 Grand Prix du roman de l'Académie française, the Prix René-Fallet, and the 1993 Prix Alain-Fournier. Unless otherwise stated, all works were originally published in French by Éditions Albin Michel.

Américo Ferreira Amorim (21 July 1934 – 13 July 2017) was a Portuguese heir and businessman. He was ranked by Forbes as the 385th richest person in the world in January 2015. His wealth was at $4.8 billion (July 2017) He was known for having a 50% interest in Corticeira Amorim. He was born in Mozelos, Santa Maria da Feira, Portugal. Amorim died on 13 July 2017 at his home in Grijo, Portugal after a short-illness, aged 82.

Amélie Mummendey (19 June 1944 – 17 December 2018) was a German social psychologist. From 2007 until her death she was a Vice-Rector for the Graduate Academy at the Friedrich Schiller University Jena. She was born in Bonn, Germany. She held a chair in social psychology at the University of Münster (1980–1997) before taking up a chair in social psychology at the Friedrich Schiller University Jena in 1997. Mummendey died on 17 December 2018 at the age of 74.

Amédée Antoine-Marie Grab (3 February 1930 – 19 May 2019) was a Swiss Roman Catholic bishop. He became a priest in 1954. He served as titular bishop of Canæ and auxiliary bishop of Lausanne, Geneva and Fribourg from 1987 to 1995. He then served as bishop of the diocese from 1995 to 1998. He then served as the bishop of Chur from 1995 to 2007. Grab was born in Zürich. Grab died on 19 May 2019, at the age of 89.

An Jung-sik (1861–1919) was an artist who lived in the late Joseon dynasty. In 1918 he organized the association of paintings and writings artists (Seohwa-hyeopae; 서화협회;書畵協會)'. And he founded Gyeongmokdang in which artists and supporters gathered and communicated with each other. As the leader of the association he made an effort to educate younger artist generation. He was excellent at landscape, portrait, flowers and birds. Gunjakdo (군작도;群雀圖). In his period, the western modern art was introduced to Korea, and the Korean traditional art was declining. He not only tried to succeed the traditional art but also adapt the western art, a realistic trend.

An An (; 1986 – 21 July 2022) was a male giant panda. He lived in Hong Kong Ocean Park. He was a gift from the Central People's Government of China to the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region in 1999. He was the longest-living male giant panda in the world under human care before his death in 2022. An An was euthanised at aged 35 on 21 July 2022 at Hong Kong Ocean Park after being sick for the last three weeks.

Ana González González, more commonly known by her married name Ana González de Recabarren (25 July 1925 – 26 October 2018), was a Chilean human rights activist. She was born in Tocopilla, Chile. González joined the Association of Relatives of the Disappeared Detainees (AFDD) and became one of its primary leaders alongside Sola Sierra, Viviana Díaz, and Clotario Blest. She participated in a hunger strike at the United Nations Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean headquarters in Santiago. In 1996, she was the focus of the Televisión Nacional de Chile-broadcast documentary Quiero llorar a mares and in 2001 won the Premios Ondas for Ibero-America for the Best Program or Professional or Television Station. In June 2000, she sued former dictator Augusto Pinochet for the disappearance of her family 26 years prior. González died from a lung infection in Santiago on 26 October 2018 at the age of 93.

Ana Castillo (born June 15, 1953) is a Chicana poet, novelist, and essayist. She writes in English. She sometimes uses Spanglish words and phrases. She was born and raised in Chicago. She writes stories about her Mexican ancestors. When she was a nine-year-old girl, she wrote her first poems about death of her Latina grandmother. Her famous books are The Invitation (1979), Women Are Not Roses (1984), and Massacre of the Dreamers (1994). She writes essays about race, sex, and gender in the United States and Mexico. She also writes science fiction.

Ana Derșidan-Ene-Pascu (22 September 1944 – 6 April 2022) was a Romanian fencer and sport leader. She won a bronze medal in the women's team foil events at the 1968 and 1972 Summer Olympics. Derșidan-Ene-Pascu was born in Bucharest, Romania. Derșidan-Ene-Pascu died on 6 April 2022 at the age of 77.

Ana Čolović Lešoska (born c.1979) is a Macedonian biologist. Since 2011, she has campaigned against the construction of dams for hydroelectric power production in the Mavrovo National Park. It was in order to protect the threatened species, including the Balkan lynx. This led to the removal of loans from the World Bank and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD). It was convincing the Government of North Macedonia to hold on the further works on dams in the national park. For her works, in April 2019, she was awarded the Goldman Environmental Prize. Colovic Lesoska heard about plans to create hydroelectric power facilities in Mavrovo in 2010. They included the 33m-high Boškov Most dam and the 70m-high Lukovo Pole dam. She was an executive director of Eko-svest. It was a Macedonian environmental research centre. It was in collaboration with other NGOs and activists. She launched the "Save Mavrovo" campaign. In November 2011, she complained about the ERBD. She explained that they had approved a loan for the Boškov Most project without conducting the required biodiversity assessment. She encouraged the ambassadors of countries with representatives on the EBRD board. She encouraged them to push for an end to the funding. A petition she launched was urging the government. They were urging the ERBD and the World Bank to bring the projects to a close. It was supported by almost 100,000 signatures. In 2013, she complained to the Berne Convention on the Conservation of European Wildlife and Natural Habitats. She explained that the Boškov Most hydropower project "could have a decisive negative impact on the lynx". In December 2015, the Berne Convention ordered the ERBD and the World Bank to hold on the financing as the project could have "a decisive negative impact on the lynx". The World Bank immediately remove funding. During the following month of May, a court decided to stop the environmental permit for the Boškov Most project. In January 2017, the EBRD cancelled financing. For her achievements, in April 2019 Ana Colovic Lesoska was given the Goldman Environmental Prize. It was the first time the prize had been awarded to a North Macedonian.

Ana Ambrazienė (14 April 1955 – 12 February 2025) was a Lithuanian hurdler. She was born in Vilnius. She represented the Soviet Union in the 1970s and 1980s. She won a silver medal at the World Athletics Championships in 1983. Ambrazienė died on 12 February 2025 in Vilnius at the age of 69.

Ana María Matute Ausejo (26 July 1925 – 25 June 2014) was a Spanish writer and member of the Real Academia Española. She is thought to have been one of the most famous writers since the Spanish Civil War. She was born in Barcelona. She studied at the international school of Hilversum in the Netherlands. She was a guest lecturer to the universities of Oklahoma, Indiana and Virginia. On 25 June 2014, Matute died of a heart attack at the age of 88, and was laid to rest in the Cemetery of Montjuïc, Barcelona.

Ana María Vela Rubio (29 October 1901 – 15 December 2017), was a Spanish supercentenarian. She is the oldest verified Spaniard ever from 6 June 2016, however now Maria Branyas Morera is holding the record for the oldest person to have ever lived in Spain. Vela Rubio was also the third-oldest living person in the world, behind Nabi Tajima and Chiyo Miyako. Vela Rubio was born 29 October 1901 in Puente Genil, Andalusia. She used to work as a dressmaker. She never married her partner as her parents did not agree to their marrying, but the couple had two children. Her daughter, also named Ana, lives with her. She became the oldest European since the death of oldest person Emma Morano on 15 April 2017. She died on 15 December 2017. Vela Rubio was succeeded as the Europe's oldest living person by Giuseppina Projetto-Frau of Italy.

Dom Anacleto Cordeiro Gonçalves de Oliveira (17 July 1946 – 18 September 2020) was a Portuguese Roman Catholic prelate. He was ordained to the priesthood in 1970. He was auxiliary bishop of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Lisbon from 2005 to 2010. He then was bishop of the Roman Catholic Diocese of Viana do Castelo, Portugal, from 2010 until his death. Oliveira died on 18 September 2020 in Lisbon from a car crash at the age of 74.

Ana Luísa Amaral (5 April 1956 – 5 August 2022) was a Portuguese poet, novelist and translator. She was a professor at the University of Porto. She was born in Lisbon, Portugal. Amaral died on 5 August 2022 in Porto, Portugal from a long illness at the age of 66.

Ananda Mohan Chakrabarty ( Ānandamōhan Cakrabartī; April 4, 1938 – July 10, 2020) was an Indian-American microbiologist and researcher. He was known for his work in directed evolution and his role in creating a genetically engineered organism using plasmid. This led to landmark Supreme Court case, Diamond v. Chakrabarty. Chakrabarty died on July 10, 2020 in Illinois, aged 82.

Ananta Charan Sukla (6 November 1942 – 1 October 2020) was an Indian educator, philosopher and historian. He was a professor of English and Comparative Literature at Sambalpur University. He was born in Odisha, India. Sukla was the founding editor of the international half-yearly Journal of Comparative Literature and Aesthetics. Sukla died on 1 October 2020 in Odisha from multiple organ failure at the age of 77.

Anatole France (; born Anatole François Thibault; 16 April 1844 – 12 October 1924) was a French writer. He wrote novels, short stories, poems and essays. He was also a famous critic. France was born in Paris. His father sold old books. The son grew up in the bookshop and loved books all his life. He began as a poet. Later he became famous for his novels. Many people of his time said he was the greatest living French writer. France liked to doubt. He did not accept big ideas without asking questions. But he also had a warm heart. He liked to repeat two words as a rule of life: "irony and pity". Irony means saying things with a hidden smile. Pity means feeling the pain of others. In 1896 he was elected to the Académie française, a body of forty members. Election to it is one of the highest honours in French literature. In 1898 he took a big risk. He defended Alfred Dreyfus, an army officer who was punished for a crime he did not commit. After that, France fought for socialist ideas and for peace. In 1921 he won the Nobel Prize in Literature. France died in 1924. The state gave him a very grand funeral. Soon after, his fame went down. Younger writers attacked his memory. His works are still studied today, though he is less widely read than in his lifetime. The writer's legal name, in the civil records of the French state, was Anatole François Thibault. He was baptised on 9 June 1844, in the church of Saint-Germain-des-Prés. The parish register of the baptism still exists; it gives the names in another order, "François-Anatole". Older books often print a third form, "Jacques Anatole François". Neither original document contains the name Jacques. The godfather at the baptism was called Jacques Charavay. He came from a family of famous dealers in old letters and autographs. His son Étienne became the boy's best school friend. "France" was not his real family name. It came from his father. The father was called François Thibault. He came from Anjou, a region in the west of France. There, people used "France" as a short, friendly form of "François". The father had carried this name since his own childhood. The father used "France" as his shop name. He was known as "Noël France" or "le père France" (Father France). The son signed his school work "Anatole France" from an early age. Later, the whole world knew him by this pen name. A pen name is a name a writer uses instead of his real name. Anatole France was born on 16 April 1844 at 19 Quai Malaquais in Paris. The house stands on the left bank of the river Seine, opposite the Louvre palace. His parents lived in the same building as their bookshop. A few months after his birth, the family and the shop moved a short distance along the same street, to number 15. His father, François Noël Thibault, was born on 25 December 1805 in Luigné, a village in Anjou. Because he was born on Christmas Day, people called him Noël, the French word for Christmas. His exact date of birth is known from his army papers, which Girard found and published. His family was very poor. His father, who was Anatole France's grandfather, made shoes in a village. As a boy, Noël began work as a farm worker. When he was a young man, he became a soldier. He joined the army freely in 1826, when he was twenty years old. He served in the royal guard of King Charles X. His friends thought that the shape of his face even looked a little like that of the king whom he admired. In August 1830, he stood in the yard of the castle at Maintenon with the soldiers to whom the fallen king said goodbye. According to a family story, he could not even read when he joined the army. He later taught himself to read. After 1830, Noël had to leave the army. He became a clerk for Téchener, an old bookseller in Paris. By 1838, he was managing a bookshop for an older bookseller. In January 1839, he became the owner of the shop. The shop was unusual. It sold books, papers, and pictures about the French Revolution. This was largely because of its best customer and protector, the comte de La Bédoyère. He was a rich nobleman who collected everything connected with the Revolution. Noël became an expert on the subject. He prepared a large catalogue of documents about the Revolution, and historians used his work. The bookshop itself became famous. The poet Gérard de Nerval mentioned it in one of his stories. A collector searching for rare books says that he must visit the learned booksellers: "there is France, there is Merlin, there is Téchener". Anatole's father was a serious man. He was a strong Catholic and a royalist. A royalist is a person who wants the country to be ruled by a king. His son later supported very different ideas. Some writers think that the endless discussions in the bookshop made the boy want to disagree with other people. His grandmother also felt close to the France that had existed before the Revolution. His mother, Antoinette Gallas, was born in Chartres on 1 November 1811. No father was named in the official record of her birth. She was already a widow when she married Noël France. Her first husband, a pharmacist, had died young. The wedding took place on 29 February 1840, a date that exists only during a leap year. Antoinette was quick and lively, while her husband was slow and calm. She loved her only son very deeply. France later said that he had received his gift for telling stories from her. He also said, partly as a joke, that she watched him too closely, even after he had become an adult. In 1853, the family moved a short distance to the Quai Voltaire. Their new bookshop was at number 9. Both the Quai Malaquais and the Quai Voltaire run beside the Seine. They contain many shops that sell old books, old pictures, and old works of art. These streets became the boy's first school. He walked beside the river and looked into every shop window. He also carried messages and objects for his father. On the way, he stopped to read books placed in open boxes outside the shops. He kept this habit throughout his life. Inside his father's shop, he listened to old collectors talking about the French Revolution. Their conversations stayed in his memory. Sixty years later, they helped him write his great novel about the Revolution, The Gods Are Athirst. When he was seven years old, the religious little boy wrote a book called "Christian Thoughts". On its first page, he wrote that the author was too young to have the book printed and would wait until he was twenty. France later wrote about his childhood in several books. The best known are Le Livre de mon ami (My Friend's Book, 1885) and Pierre Nozière (1899). In these works, he changed some of the facts. For example, he turned his bookseller father into a doctor named Nozière. France said that the feelings in the books were true, even when the details were not. Anatole was first sent for a short time to a small boarding school in Versailles. From 1853, he attended a small Catholic school called the Institution Sainte-Marie in the rue Bonaparte. He went there during the day and returned home in the evening. In 1855, he entered the Collège Stanislas, a well-known Catholic school in Paris. He arrived in October, when he was eleven and a half years old. He was not a good pupil in most subjects, and his marks were poor. One teacher described him as careless and lazy. The teacher's notes still exist in a cheap little notebook with a green cover. Anatole sometimes missed his lessons and spent the time in the Louvre, dreaming in front of the Greek sculptures. However, he could do very well when he wrote essays in French. The school gave prizes to several of his compositions. One of them was La Légende de sainte Radegonde (1859), the story of a holy queen. It became his first "book". The manuscript is dated 20 November 1859. A few weeks later, the boy wrote another religious story, this time about a holy woman who had been shut inside a small room. His uncle Jean-Pierre Dufour copied the text in neat, rounded handwriting. His father's shop then produced a small number of copies. The booklet had a printed cover and was dedicated "to a beloved father and a beloved mother". The fifteen-year-old writer signed it "your devoted son". Today, this small booklet is one of the rarest objects collected by people interested in French books. In 1861, another school essay brought him one of his first successes. It was a meditation on the ruins of Palmyra, an ancient city in the desert. His school years remained in his memory in an unusual way. He later gave the names of some of his teachers and classmates to characters in his books. Many years later, when France entered the Académie française, the school director Octave Gréard made a gentle joke about his years as a pupil. He said that France had been one of those pupils who did not work hard at the tasks they were given but followed a path of their own. France left the school at the end of July 1862, after completing the class of rhetoric and failing the final examination. Nobody knows exactly why he did not return. He finally passed the examination called the baccalauréat on 5 November 1864, when he was twenty years old. He had failed at least once before, and a family story says that he had failed several times. He took the examination beside his best friend from school, Étienne Charavay, the son of his godfather, and wrote joking verses about the experience. For about twelve years, France had no regular job. He lived on small pieces of literary work. He wrote notes about books, articles for magazines, and entries for dictionaries. He signed some of these short texts with the name "Vicomte d'Elotana". This strange name is simply "Anatole" written backwards. In 1862, France and his father worked together on a large project. The comte de La Bédoyère, a great collector and an old protector of the family bookshop, had died. In his will, he ordered "France the bookseller" to prepare a catalogue of his enormous library about the French Revolution. France's father knew the books, while the son wrote the introduction and many of the notes. While working among this great mass of old papers, the young man came very close to the world of the French Revolution. Fifty years later, that world became the subject of his novel The Gods Are Athirst. The young man's political ideas were already very different from those of his royalist father. During the Second Empire of Napoleon III, he quietly supported the republican opposition. Between 1867 and 1870, he wrote for small magazines for people who loved books. In them, he praised the Revolution and made fun of the Empire. Sometimes he hid his attacks inside poems about tyrants from the ancient world. In 1868, with the poet Louis-Xavier de Ricard, he even announced a great Encyclopedia of the Revolution in twelve volumes. Famous republican writers promised to write parts of it, but only the short paper announcing the plan was ever printed. During these years, France also had his first unhappy love. One evening in 1861, his parents took him to the theatre as a reward for good school work. At the Comédie-Française, he saw the actress Élise Devoyod on the stage and fell in love with her. For years, he loved her from a distance. Once, he even watched her while she prayed in the church of Saint-Roch. In July 1865, he finally found the courage to write to her. The love had no hope of success, and he placed his pain into poems that were never published. The memory returned much later in his novel Les Désirs de Jean Servien, in which a poor young man loves a famous actress from a distance. The figure of the distant actress remained in France's work. She appears again in the first poem about Thaïs in 1867, in Histoire comique, and even in The Gods Are Athirst. In August 1864, France played a famous trick. He published ten lines of verse in a small learned magazine called L'Intermédiaire des chercheurs et curieux. The lines appeared on 10 August 1864. He said that they were lost lines by the poet André Chénier. In fact, France had written them himself. Even Chénier's own nephew believed the story and included the false lines in an edition of his uncle's poems. Becq de Fouquières, the greatest expert on Chénier at that time, was also fooled. The young writer was already able to copy the style of older masters very well. For a time, he also earned some money as a teacher. He taught at a private school in Ivry, just south of Paris, called the Institution Sigisbert Pompée. He did not speak much about this work later. However, he remembered the place. In 1869, he signed some articles with the name "Camille d'Ivry". For years, France's father waited for his son to take control of the bookshop. Anatole refused because he wanted to write books, not sell them. In June 1866, his father was ill and finally gave up the idea. He sold the business. In 1868, France published his first true book. It was a short study of the poet Alfred de Vigny. Around 1867, the poet Catulle Mendès introduced France to a group of young poets called the Parnassians. These poets loved ancient Greece and Rome. They wanted poetry to be calm, perfect, and carefully made, like a marble statue. They were against the strong and open emotions of the older Romantic poets. France joined this group. He went to the private meetings held by its leader, the poet Leconte de Lisle. A salon is a group of people who meet often in a private home to talk about art and ideas. At the beginning of 1867, France had also joined a very small magazine for young poets called La Gazette rimée. It never had more than thirty-eight readers who paid for it. Paul Verlaine was one of the other writers in the magazine. In 1867, France published a poem called La Légende de sainte Thaïs. More than twenty years later, this early subject became his famous novel Thaïs. The publisher of the Parnassian poets was Alphonse Lemerre. From 1869, France worked for Lemerre as a reader of manuscripts. He earned about 150 francs each month. He also prepared editions of older French writers for Lemerre. In 1874, he wrote a long study of Racine. This slow and careful work as an editor became his true school of writing style. His own poems appeared in the Parnassian collection Le Parnasse contemporain. One of them, "La Part de Madeleine", was read aloud in public by the actress Agar and had great success. A friend later remembered that, in those days, such a public reading could make a young man accepted as a real poet. In July 1870, war began between France and Prussia. The young writer remained in Paris. In October, during the siege of the city, he was called into the National Guard, the army made up of ordinary citizens. In January 1871, an army group decided that he did not have to continue serving. In the spring came the Commune, a violent workers' revolt that took control of Paris. France did not join it. On 5 May 1871, he left the city with false papers and hid with friends in the countryside until the fighting ended. The violence and killing frightened him. For many years afterwards, his political ideas remained careful and moderate. In 1873, Lemerre published France's first collection of poems, Les Poèmes dorés (Golden Poems). The poems describe nature, animals, and scenes from the ancient world in a calm and carefully polished style. One scholar has shown that behind these poems about animals was a young man's dream that all forms of life were joined together. This idea was influenced by the natural science of his time. During these years, France also met the novelist Gustave Flaubert. In 1875, the Parnassian poets prepared their third and final collection. France was a member of the small group that chose which poems would be included. The older poets Théodore de Banville and François Coppée were also members. The group rejected poems by Paul Verlaine and Charles Cros. It also rejected a long poem by Stéphane Mallarmé, "L'Après-midi d'un faune". France is said to have written one short sentence about Mallarmé's poem: "they would laugh at us". Later history judged the judges badly. The poets who had been rejected became some of the greatest names in French poetry, and Mallarmé's Faune became one of the most famous French poems. France himself later made peace with this part of his past. In 1893, he publicly praised Mallarmé in the newspaper Le Temps. In 1876, France published a second book of poetry, Les Noces corinthiennes (The Bride of Corinth). It is a play in verse set in ancient Greece, at the time when Christianity was new. A young woman is promised to God by her Christian mother. This promise destroys the girl's love and finally her life. The poem already shows one of the main ideas that remained in France's work throughout his life: religion can be beautiful, but it can also destroy human happiness. One important writer stood behind the work: Ernest Renan, the historian of religion whom France had read for many years. France's poem about Mary Magdalene, written in 1869, had already been strongly influenced by Renan. The old writer George Sand, near the end of her own life, wrote a letter to the young poet. She said that his work was beautiful and fresh like ancient art, and that it had made her cry. The work was first performed for the public only in 1902. Before that, it had been performed once at a private evening in 1884. After this book, France almost stopped writing poetry. Prose became his true form of writing. Leconte de Lisle had already understood this. Around 1874, the older poet had said that this student of poetry would become a good writer of prose. On 3 August 1876, France received a small job in the library of the French Senate, in the Luxembourg Palace in Paris. He was paid 2,200 francs a year. He had first asked for a job there ten years earlier, in 1866. His father had even written a letter to support his request, but it had failed. The job gave him enough money to live, but he did not like it. He was only a junior assistant. The head librarian was the writer Charles-Edmond. He was a Polish count who had become a French writer and was one of the founders of the newspaper Le Temps. When France had first asked for a job in 1866, Charles-Edmond had answered with one unkind word: "Néant", meaning nothing. Ten years later, Charles-Edmond himself proposed that France should receive the job. He also allowed the young writer to publish in Le Temps, where France's first articles appeared in 1875. The poet Leconte de Lisle, who already worked in the library, had also strongly supported his young friend. The work was not difficult. France only had to spend a few hours each week preparing records of books. Even so, he often arrived late, left early, and did as little work as possible. His final years at the library were unhappy. In 1888, a better job there became free. France hoped to receive it, but it was given to a younger man. France protested, but nothing changed. His relations with Charles-Edmond became worse and worse. Someone once asked Charles-Edmond to write a report about the work France had done during six years. The old librarian again answered with one word: nothing. France left the job on 1 February 1890. By that time, he no longer needed the salary. One amusing detail remains: he wrote the first version of his novel Thaïs on official paper from the Senate library. On 28 April 1877, France married Valérie Guérin de Sauville. They had a civil wedding at the town hall of the sixth district of Paris and a religious wedding at the church of Saint-Sulpice. Valérie was twenty years old, while France was almost thirty-three. Charles-Edmond and the publisher Lemerre were witnesses at the wedding. Valérie's family was proud of its name. Several generations of the family had been painters. One of them, Jean Guérin, had painted fine small portraits of Queen Marie Antoinette. Valérie's father was an important clerk at the Ministry of Finance. The couple lived in Neuilly, which was then a quiet suburb of Paris that still seemed almost like the countryside. At first, they seem to have lived there in the house of Valérie's father. Their only child, a daughter named Suzanne, was born on 1 March 1881. France loved her deeply and wrote gentle pages about small children. With Valérie's dowry, the money that a bride brought into a marriage, the family bought a small house in the Rue Chalgrin. The marriage was not happy. France and Valérie had very different characters. In June 1892, France left the family home. Their divorce became official on 2 August 1893, and the court said that France was responsible for the failure of the marriage. Valérie kept the house and continued to care for Suzanne. France had to pay her money every month. France began writing fiction in prose when he was in his thirties. In 1878, his first novel, Jocaste, appeared as a serial in the newspaper Le Temps. A serial is a story published in parts over several days or weeks. The newspaper printed the story without giving the author's name. In 1879, Jocaste was published as a book together with a second short novel, Le Chat maigre (The Skinny Cat). France dedicated Le Chat maigre to Charles-Edmond as a small sign of thanks and affection. The publisher was Calmann Lévy. This company remained France's main publisher for the rest of his life. His decision to change publishers angered his former publisher, Lemerre. In a contract signed in 1878, France had promised to give Lemerre several works, including a short history of France. France gave him the manuscript in 1882, but Lemerre did not publish it. The two men then argued about money for many years. Thirty years later, Lemerre suddenly decided that he wanted to publish the old book. France no longer wanted it to appear, so he went to court to stop him. France won the case in November 1911. France's first great success came in April 1881 with Le Crime de Sylvestre Bonnard (The Crime of Sylvestre Bonnard). The main character is an old scholar who lives alone among his books. His "crime" is really an act of kindness. He takes a poor young girl away from a cruel school in order to save her. Sylvestre Bonnard is gentle, learned, and full of quiet irony. He is the first of several wise old men who appear in France's books. After him came Jérôme Coignard, Monsieur Bergeret, and Brotteaux. One English critic wrote that the kind thinker who would later defend Dreyfus was already present in this novel of 1881. The book pleased serious critics such as Hippolyte Taine, and it was also popular with the public. In 1882, the Académie française gave it a prize. France had now become a well-known name in French literature. In 1881, he also became the literary adviser of the Charavay publishing house. It was the family company of his godfather and of his school friend Étienne. In 1882, Lemerre published Les Désirs de Jean Servien, a darker story about the hopeless dreams of a poor young man. In 1883 came Abeille, a fairy tale for children, published by the Charavay company. In 1885, France published Le Livre de mon ami (My Friend's Book), a gentle book of childhood memories. A few months earlier, at the very end of 1884, the French state had made him a knight of the Legion of Honour, the country's national order. From March 1883, France also wrote a column every two weeks for the magazine L'Univers illustré. He used the pen name "Gérôme" and continued this work until 1896. "Gérôme" was a name used by the magazine rather than by one writer alone. France and another writer used it in turn, so readers could not know which of them had written each article. France now earned money from his books, his magazine column, and his work at the library. Because of this, he no longer had serious money problems. In 1883, France also met the man he admired more than any other, Ernest Renan. He began to be welcomed into Renan's home. Renan was a famous scholar of religion. He had left the Catholic faith and studied the life of Jesus as a subject of history rather than as a matter of belief. France always called Renan his master. In 1886, the major newspaper Le Temps gave France a weekly column about life in Paris. The first article appeared on 21 March 1886. Two months later, his mother died. In January 1887, the column received a new title, "La Vie littéraire" (The Literary Life). From then on, France reviewed the new books published each week. He became one of the most powerful literary critics in Paris. The best of these articles were collected in four books called La Vie littéraire, published between 1888 and 1892. One American writer said that France's years at Le Temps made him the leader of French literature. When Renan died in 1892, France took his place as the leading writer of the country. France had his own idea of literary criticism. He did not believe that books could be judged in a cold and scientific way. He thought that a critic could only explain what a book did to the critic's own mind. In a famous sentence, he said that a good critic tells "the adventures of his soul among masterpieces". He added that there was no objective criticism, just as there was no objective art. Here, "objective" means judged without personal feelings. Other critics attacked this idea. The serious professor Ferdinand Brunetière, more than anyone else, argued against France in long public debates. However, readers liked France's method. His articles were small works of art: light, learned, and full of charm. France did not like the heavy realism of Émile Zola. In August 1887, he attacked Zola's novel La Terre in one of the strongest and most violent articles he ever wrote. However, he could also judge the same writer fairly. He honestly praised Zola's power and the great size of his work. This fairness became important later, when the two men fought on the same side during the Dreyfus affair. France was first introduced to Madame Arman de Caillavet in 1883, but she was not impressed by him. In the summer of 1886, her husband invited France to Capian, the family's country home. In 1888, their friendship became the most important relationship of France's life. He fell in love with Léontine Arman de Caillavet. She had been born Léontine Lippmann in 1844 and was the daughter of a rich banker. She was married to Albert Arman de Caillavet. They had a son named Gaston, who was born in 1869. Madame de Caillavet held a famous literary salon in Paris. A salon was a regular meeting where writers, artists, and important people came together to talk. She received guests every Sunday and gave dinners every Wednesday. France became the most famous guest in her home. The young Marcel Proust, who greatly admired France, was one of the visitors. In 1896, France wrote the preface to Proust's first book, Les Plaisirs et les Jours. Madame de Caillavet did much more than welcome France into her home. She made him work. France was slow and often lazy when working on large projects. She encouraged him, watched his progress, and kept him at his desk. She acted as his translator, adviser, and judge. She even wrote down things that he said at the dinner table so that he could use them in future books. She gave herself completely to helping his fame and career. Dargan compares her care for France with the help that Madame Récamier gave to the old Chateaubriand. Her help went very far. She sometimes wrote complete pages that were published under France's name. These included part of a preface and several newspaper articles. Her daughter-in-law spoke openly about this many years later. From 1893, France and Madame de Caillavet also travelled together during almost every summer. They went most often to Italy. A younger friend, the writer Nicolas Ségur, later said that without her, Le Lys rouge would never have been written. He also believed that some of France's other novels would have stopped after only ten pages. With her help, France published book after book during the ten years after 1888. His love for her changed both his way of thinking and his working habits. One scholar explained the change in this way: France's doubt had once protected him, but it later became a doubt that attacked. Thaïs appeared as a serial in 1889 and as a book in October 1890. The serial ran in the Revue des Deux Mondes, the most respected review in France. A few months before the book, in May 1890, France's old father died. The story of the novel happens in Egypt in the early centuries of Christianity. Paphnuce, a proud desert monk, decides to save the soul of Thaïs, a beautiful actress of Alexandria. He succeeds: she enters a convent and dies a saint. But he fails himself. Desire and doubt destroy him, and at the end he understands that his whole faith may have been vanity. The novel turns a pious old legend upside down, with quiet irony. It also shows France's love of the ancient world and its wisdom. The book was a great success. In 1894 the composer Jules Massenet made it into a famous opera, first played at the Paris Opera on 16 March 1894. France also wrote many short stories. Balthasar (1889) retells the story of one of the three kings of the Bible. L'Étui de nacre (Mother of Pearl, 1892) contains some of his most famous tales. One of them, "Le Jongleur de Notre-Dame", was first printed in the newspaper Le Gaulois on 10 May 1890, as a "tale for the month of May". It tells of Barnabé, a poor juggler turned monk, who honours the Virgin Mary with the only thing he can do: his juggling tricks. France had found the old miracle story in a book of 1888 on the French literature of the Middle Ages, by the scholar Gaston Paris, and he dedicated his tale to him. In 1902 the tale gave Massenet the subject of a second opera, after Thaïs. Readers have long been surprised by the warm, pious tone of this story from the great doubter. A recent study argues that such moments of religious "purity" are no accident, but a true and lasting part of his work. Another, "Le Procurateur de Judée", shows an old Roman governor, Pontius Pilate, who cannot even remember Jesus. In 1893 came La Rôtisserie de la reine Pédauque (At the Sign of the Reine Pédauque). The story had first run as a weekly serial in the newspaper L'Écho de Paris, from October to December 1892. The story is set in the Paris of the 18th century. Its hero is the abbé Jérôme Coignard, a fat, learned, drunken and lovable priest. He is full of wisdom and full of sins at the same time. In this book France plays with the free, laughing spirit of Rabelais. A second book, Les Opinions de M. Jérôme Coignard (1893), collects the abbé's ideas about kings, war, justice, money and academies. Under the old costume, the ideas are sharp comments on modern France. Madame de Caillavet wanted France to write a modern love novel, the kind that high society read. The result was Le Lys rouge (The Red Lily, 1894). He began it in 1893 under another title, "La Terre des morts". Madame de Caillavet then organised a journey to Florence, so that the most tender pages could be set in real places. She left one Thursday in May and took France, her son and her new daughter-in-law with her. The novel follows Thérèse, a rich married woman, and her painful love for the sculptor Dechartre, in Paris and in Florence. The red lily is the flower of Florence. Many readers have seen in the book a mirror of France's own passion at that time. In 1899 it was turned into a play, acted by the stars Réjane and Lucien Guitry. In the same year 1894 France published a very different book: Le Jardin d'Épicure (The Garden of Epicurus). It is a collection of short thoughts about life, death, science, love and books. Epicurus was an ancient Greek thinker who taught calm pleasure and freedom from fear. The book is the clearest window into France's own mind. It contains his famous appeal to irony and pity as guides through life. A last collection of Italian tales, Le Puits de sainte Claire (The Well of Saint Clare), followed in 1895. In August 1894 France used his new wealth to buy a private house at 5 Villa Saïd, near the Bois de Boulogne in Paris. He paid 70,000 francs for it. On 23 January 1896 France was elected to the Académie française. This body brings together forty writers and scholars. Election to it is one of the highest honours in French literature. He won at the first vote, with 21 votes out of 34; his main rival, the journalist Francis Charmes, received 12. He took the seat of Ferdinand de Lesseps, the builder of the Suez Canal. The formal reception took place on 24 December 1896. The director Octave Gréard welcomed him with an elegant speech, joking about the new member's love story with ancient Egypt and its queens. As the custom was, a volume of selected pages from the new member's works then appeared. The scholar Gustave Lanson, who chose the pages, noted that ancient Greece had shaped France's mind even more deeply than Rome. France was fifty-two. He had reached the top of official glory. Two years later, he put all this glory at risk. In 1894 a French army captain, Alfred Dreyfus, was found guilty of selling secrets to Germany. He was sent to a prison island for life. Dreyfus was Jewish, and hatred of Jews played a large part in the case. In fact, he was innocent. The real spy was another officer. For years, most French people believed the army. Only a small group asked questions. The fight over Dreyfus, called the Dreyfus affair, split families and friends. It became a fight about justice itself. Doubts about the trial spread in the summer of 1897. On 23 November 1897 the newspaper L'Aurore asked France for his opinion. He answered that he could not judge Dreyfus guilty while the documents of the case stayed secret. He did not even doubt, he said, since nobody had shown him one page of the file. In careful words, this was a demand for a new trial. Behind the careful public words, the sceptic went to work. He questioned two masters of old papers: his school friend Étienne Charavay, the autograph expert, and the head of the École des Chartes. He asked them what handwriting reports were really worth, and came back troubled. At the end of November or early in December, young defenders of Dreyfus brought a first list of names to his door. France left his bed, wrapped up against a cold, and said he would sign everything: he was revolted. That first paper gathered too few names and was never published. On 7 January 1898 the secret paper of the charges of 1894 was at last printed. France read it, and his hesitation turned into conviction. On 13 January 1898 Émile Zola published his famous open letter J'accuse in L'Aurore. The next day the paper printed a petition asking for a new trial. Zola signed first. Anatole France signed second. Young supporters of Dreyfus had asked him for his name. Years later, two of them, Marcel Proust and the poet Fernand Gregh, each claimed the honour of having collected his signature. France signed knowing what it might cost him. He repeated: "It must be done. Dreyfus is innocent." He was the only member of the Académie française to take a public stand for Dreyfus. Enemies mocked the signers as "the Intellectuals"; the nickname stuck. On 19 February 1898 France spoke for Zola at Zola's trial. Before the court, he praised Zola's admirable good faith and absolute sincerity. Outside, a crowd howled against the accused. Later that year he signed first on a protest for Colonel Picquart, the officer who had found the truth and now sat in prison himself. In July 1898 Zola was struck off the roll of the Legion of Honour; France then stopped wearing his own decoration. He became a close friend of the socialist leader Jean Jaurès. He was one of the first members of the League of the Rights of Man, a new group formed to defend justice. The price was high. He received insults in public and in private. Old friends such as the writers Maurice Barrès and Charles Maurras broke with him. Crowds sometimes gathered before his house to shout at him. The guest list of Madame de Caillavet's salon changed almost completely. The direction of the affair changed in August 1898, when an officer admitted he had forged a key document. A new trial was held at Rennes in 1899. Absurdly, the judges again found Dreyfus guilty, but "with extenuating circumstances": facts, the court said, that made the crime look less serious. Dreyfus was pardoned, and only years later fully cleared. When Zola died suddenly in 1902, France spoke over his coffin, on 5 October, before a huge crowd. In fighting for justice, he said, Zola had been "a moment in the conscience of mankind". In July 1906, when the innocent man, restored to the army, received the Legion of Honour in a military ceremony, France was present and came to congratulate him. France himself had left the anti-Dreyfus paper L'Écho de Paris at the beginning of 1899; in July of that year he moved his weekly work to the pro-Dreyfus Le Figaro. France also turned away from his own Academy. He was the only declared Dreyfusard among the forty members, and from 1900 he simply stopped attending its meetings. He stayed away for sixteen years. Why did the calm sceptic enter this dangerous fight? France himself saw more than one man's fate in the case. Behind the injustice he saw the power of the army and the Church over the Republic. A South American critic wrote that the doubter simply took the side of reason and justice. For France, the affair was a test of the whole nation. While the affair raged, France wrote it into fiction, almost week by week. Since January 1895 he had been printing short newspaper chapters about life in a small French town. These chapters grew into a series of four novels called L'Histoire contemporaine (Contemporary History): L'Orme du mail (The Elm-Tree on the Mall, 1897) Le Mannequin d'osier (The Wicker-Work Woman, 1897) L'Anneau d'améthyste (The Amethyst Ring, 1899) Monsieur Bergeret à Paris (Monsieur Bergeret in Paris, 1901) The hero, Monsieur Bergeret, is a gentle professor of Latin. In the first books he sits under an elm tree or in a bookshop and talks with priests, officers and officials about the small plots of the town. His wife betrays him; the world laughs at him; he thinks for himself. Then the Dreyfus affair enters the story. In January 1898 readers of the serial met a violent, ruined officer called Raoul Marcien: a barely hidden portrait of the real traitor, Esterhazy. Bergeret becomes a Dreyfusard, like his author. From book to book, he turns into France's own double. Writing a novel from the daily news, while the news was still happening, was a bold experiment. In 1901 France published one of his most loved stories, "Crainquebille", first called "L'Affaire Crainquebille". The first edition, at the very end of 1901, was a fine illustrated book, with pictures by the artist Théophile Steinlen. Crainquebille is a poor old street seller of vegetables in Paris. A policeman wrongly accuses him of an insult. In court, nobody listens to him. He goes to prison without understanding why. The story is the Dreyfus affair in miniature, moved to the world of the poor. It asks a simple question: can a small man get justice? France shows that Crainquebille cannot even speak the language of the judges. The critic Roberto Giusti called the tale "a masterpiece of simplicity, humour, observation and tenderness". In 1903 France turned the story into a play. The great actor Lucien Guitry played Crainquebille. The Dreyfus affair changed France's life. Through Jaurès and the long fight for Dreyfus, he moved closer to socialism. Socialism includes many different ideas, but socialists generally want workers and society to have more control over wealth and industry. France treated socialism mainly as a moral hope, not as a complete theory of history and economics. It followed the old French dreamers of the 19th century more than Karl Marx.

Anatol Hrytskievich (; January 31, 1929 – January 20, 2015) was a Belarusian historian. He was a correspondent member of the International Academy of Science of Eurasia (1996–2015), doctor of history (1986–2015), professor (1987–2015). He was born in Minsk. Hrytskievich died on January 20, 2015 in Minsk, aged 85.

Anatoli Kuzmich Grishin (; 8 July 1939 – 14 June 2016) was a Soviet sprint canoeist who competed in the mid-1960s. He won a gold medal in the K-4 1000 m event at the 1964 Summer Olympics in Tokyo.
